_readme.covers: Foundational harmonic syntax from Units 1-5, plus the early expansions (I6, V6, ii6) that appear in Unit 7, plus modal variants of the dominant in minor keys. Every meaningful root-motion pair is listed.
_readme.structure: Each rule has: id, quality, from, to, feedback.

matching.from: Root numerals for the previous chord. Empty list means the rule applies only to the very first chord of the passage.
matching.to: Root numerals for the current chord.
matching.bare_root: A bare numeral like 'V' matches any inversion of V.
matching.figured: A rule's 'to' list can include figured chords like 'I6' to match that specific inversion.
matching.sus: Suspended chords (Vsus4, V7sus4, ...) are normalised to their base form for matching, so 'V' matches both V and Vsus4.
matching.case: Uppercase and lowercase are distinguished. In minor keys the analyzer emits uppercase VII for the natural (modal) subtonic and lowercase vii for the raised (harmonic-minor) leading tone; 'v' is the Dorian minor dominant.

how_to_add_a_rule: 1. Copy a rule block between { and }.
2. Give it a new unique id.
3. Set from and to as above.
4. Pick a quality: excellent, good, fair, discouraged, bad.
6. Save. No trailing comma after the last rule.

rules.feedback: Beginning on the tonic states the key unambiguously. The listener knows immediately where home is, and the piece can depart from a place of certainty.
A predominant opening leaves the key slightly ambiguous. The music must establish the tonic quickly or the listener will feel adrift.
Opening on the dominant is uncommon in tonal music. The key is not yet established, so move to I soon.
Beginning on a mediant is weak because the key is not yet defined. This opening only works when the harmony is deliberately obscured.
Opening on the leading-tone triad is unstable. First-inversion vii° is more idiomatic than root position.
This is not a conventional opening chord. It may work in an unusual style but for a standard exercise it will feel unmoored.
Tonic to dominant. This is the fundamental harmonic motion of tonal music — root motion by descending 5th, the strongest pull the system has.
Dominant to tonic. Root motion by 4th (the inversion of a 5th). The arrival at the tonic after a dominant is the fundamental close.
Tonic to subdominant. Another descending-5th relation. The subdominant sits where the tonic can move forward without losing its identity.
Subdominant to tonic. Root motion by 5th, the mirror of V-I but without the leading tone. Softer than an authentic close.
Subdominant to dominant. Root motion by step but with the pull of a 5th underneath. The standard pre-cadential preparation.
Supertonic to dominant. Another descending-5th relation. Together with V-I, this forms the complete ii-V-I chain that underlies most cadences.
Tonic to supertonic. Opens the predominant area. The bass rises a step, setting up a stepwise approach to the cadence.
Deceptive motion. The dominant avoids the tonic and lands on vi (VI in minor), delaying closure. Often launches a phrase extension.
Submediant to supertonic. Two steps down the circle of fifths. Root motion by descending 4th continues the strong forward direction.
Supertonic to leading-tone triad. Both chords share the supertonic and subdominant, so the connection is smooth but the direction feels stalled.
Leading-tone triad to tonic. The leading tone rises to 1 in the upper voice or in the bass. Textbook contrapuntal resolution.
Leading-tone triad to dominant. The leading tone fails to resolve. Because both chords contain the leading tone, the motion sounds circular.
Leading-tone triad to submediant. Deceptive motion. The leading tone resolves up to 1 of vi, giving a soft landing.
Tonic to its own first inversion. Bass moves 1 to 3. The chord is prolonged while the bass picks up melodic motion.
First-inversion tonic back to root position. Bass steps 3 to 1. Idiomatic close of a tonic expansion.
I6 to V6 as a neighbor motion. Bass steps 3 to 7 and back. Idiomatic expansion of the tonic.
V6 to I. Bass 7 rises to 1. One of the smoothest ways to close a phrase without the weight of root-position V.
V6 to root-position V. Bass moves 7 to 5. Clear harmonic arrival after the contrapuntal first-inversion stage.
Root-position V to V6. Prolongs dominant harmony while the bass picks up motion. Fine mid-phrase, weak at cadences.
Tonic to V6 as a neighboring chord. The bass steps 1 to 7 and returns, adding motion to a tonic prolongation.
I6 to ii6. Bass 3 to 4 is a step upward. Idiomatic stepwise approach to the cadential supertonic.
Tonic to ii6. Approaching the cadential supertonic from a fresh tonic. The bass steps up, opening the predominant area.
Root-position supertonic to its first inversion. Bass steps 2 to 4. Idiomatic expansion of supertonic harmony.
Supertonic first inversion back to root position. Acceptable mid-phrase. Avoid at cadences.
Subdominant to its first inversion. Bass steps 4 to 6. Adds melodic activity to a subdominant prolongation.
Subdominant first inversion back to root. Bass steps 6 to 4. Fine mid-phrase, weaker at cadences.
IV to V6. Bass steps 4 to 7. Contrapuntal approach to the dominant that avoids a root-position arrival.
V6 to vi. Bass 7 rises to 1 while the upper voices slide into the submediant. A deceptive motion in first inversion.
Tonic to submediant first inversion. The bass steps 1 to 6, giving a smooth descent into the mediant area.
I6 to IV6. Bass 3 to 6 is a descending step. Smooth expansion of tonic into subdominant.
Mediant to dominant. The bass leaps a third down. Works but iii rarely feels like a real point of departure.
Mediant to subdominant. Rare outside of sequences. The ear hears the motion as unfocused.
Mediant to submediant. Root motion by descending 4th continues the circle of fifths.
Tonic to submediant. The two chords share two tones, so the motion is smooth and the tonic is prolonged rather than left.
Submediant to dominant. Bass steps 6 to 5. Common as a substitute for ii-V and idiomatic in the major mode.
Submediant to subdominant. Backward motion in the circle of fifths. The direction feels weak, but the shared tones make it smooth.
Submediant to tonic. Both chords share two tones, so the motion is smooth but does not create a strong sense of arrival.
Tonic to mediant. The two chords share so many tones that the motion sounds like a prolongation rather than a departure.
Mediant to tonic. The ear does not hear iii as a real goal, so the return to I feels arbitrary rather than earned.
Mediant to supertonic. Both chords are weak in isolation and the motion is a step down. Unclear function.
Subdominant to mediant. Rarely used. The direction is unclear, and iii cannot serve as a goal.
Subdominant to supertonic. Both are predominant chords, so the direction is backwards.
Supertonic to mediant. Both chords are weak in root position. The motion works in sequence but not as a functional progression.
Supertonic to submediant. The bass leaps down a fourth, which is idiomatic, but vi is a weak goal.
Dominant to subdominant is a retrogression — the reverse of the circle of fifths. The dominant's forward pull is negated.
Dominant to supertonic is a retrogression. ii should lead into V, not follow it.
Dominant to supertonic first inversion. A retrogression in the circle of fifths. The dominant should push forward, not back.
Dominant to mediant. The dominant is expected to resolve to I or vi. iii shares two tones with V, so the motion sounds indecisive.
Supertonic first inversion to tonic. Bass steps 4 to 1. The supertonic wants to lead into V, not back into I.
Supertonic first inversion to tonic first inversion. Both chords are approached by step but the direction is backwards.
Supertonic to first-inversion tonic. Retrogression. ii should lead into V, not return to a I6.
Supertonic to tonic. The bass typically steps down, which sounds weak. ii should lead to V, not return to I.
Supertonic first inversion to subdominant. Backward motion within the predominant area. Both chords have subdominant function, so the direction feels redundant.
V6 to subdominant. The bass of V6 (leading tone) must continue by step to I. Going backward to a predominant leaves the leading tone unresolved.
Mediant to dominant. The bass leaps a sixth. Works but is less smooth than ii-V or IV-V.
Subdominant to submediant. A retrogression in the circle of fifths. Both chords are subdominant-function, so the direction feels backwards.
iii is the weakest diatonic triad because it shares two tones with both I and V. Arriving on iii feels unresolved.
Root-position vii° contains a tritone above the bass, which sounds unstable. First inversion is much more idiomatic.
Leading-tone triad to mediant. Both chords share two tones, so the motion is smooth, but the arrival on iii is weak.
Leading-tone triad to subdominant. The bass leaps up a fourth. Functionally odd since vii° wants to resolve to I.
Tonic repeated. Prolongs the key without motion. Fine at a phrase opening or in a pedal, static in the middle.
Dominant repeated. Prolongs tension. The ear expects the dominant to resolve, not repeat.
Minor dominant resolving to tonic — a modal (Dorian) colouring that softens the leading-tone pull of the major dominant. Idiomatic in modal and folk-influenced writing.
Tonic to the minor dominant. The lowered seventh substitutes for the leading tone, giving a modal rather than functional dominant.
Minor dominant to submediant. A deceptive motion in the modal (Dorian) idiom, common in modal and Renaissance-influenced music.
Subtonic to tonic — a modal cadence. The lowered seventh approaches the tonic by whole step rather than by the leading-tone half step. Idiomatic in modal, folk, and Renaissance-derived writing.

Subtonic seventh resolving to tonic. The chord looks like a dominant seventh but lacks the leading tone, so the resolution is modal rather than functional. Common in Baroque and nineteenth-century writing, and a hallmark of the descending-fifths sequence.
Minor (modal) dominant to tonic — a Dorian or Aeolian cadence. Without the raised leading tone, the resolution is softer than a harmonic-minor V–i.
Tonic to minor (modal) dominant. The ear hears the dominant degree without the leading-tone pull of a major V; a Dorian-flavoured motion.
Minor dominant to minor subdominant — a Dorian motion. The chord moves against the expected functional flow, but is idiomatic in modal contexts and folk-influenced writing.
Minor subdominant to minor (modal) dominant. Dorian-flavoured stepwise motion into the modal dominant.
Mediant to subtonic — ♭III to ♭VII in the home mode. A modal step-down, idiomatic in modal and folk-influenced writing; less common in functional common-practice harmony.
Minor subdominant to subtonic. The motion prepares a modal cadence on i (or I) using the lowered seventh degree.
The same chord is repeated. Fine for prolongation; otherwise static.
A neutral transition. There is no strong functional pull in either direction.
